name: Eclipse Tidefall
description: Eclipse Tidefall orbits in the shadow of a massive gas giant companion, experiencing regular eclipses that plunge the small ocean world into darkness for hours at a time. The tidal forces from its giant neighbor create enormous standing waves that circle the planet in predictable patterns, rising and falling like the breath of the ocean itself. Between eclipses, the ruddy light reflected from the gas giant paints the seas in shades of copper and rose.

During eclipse periods, the ocean transforms. Trillions of bioluminescent plankton activate in the darkness, turning the sea surface into a glowing canvas of blue and green light that is visible from orbit. The effect is so intense that the planet appears to generate its own light, a false dawn that fades only when the true star reemerges. The air during these periods is cool and still, carrying the ozone tang of activated marine chemistry.

The microbial ecosystem of Eclipse Tidefall has evolved entirely around the eclipse cycle, with distinct light-phase and dark-phase communities that trade dominance in a rhythmic succession. The bioluminescent plankton produce light through a chemical process that also generates trace amounts of complex organic molecules, the building blocks of more advanced life that has not yet emerged. Scientists consider the planet a living laboratory for studying the early stages of biogenesis.

Eclipse Tidefall's scientific value is immense but its economic potential is limited, leading to a perpetual struggle for research funding. The standing wave patterns make surface operations hazardous, requiring specially designed floating platforms that ride the waves rather than resist them. A proposal to establish a permanent marine biology station has been pending approval for three years, caught in bureaucratic tides of its own.
